en: The *gaṇḍī* should be known as being of four types according to the distinctions of the monastic communities and their dwellings;
it is one hundred and twenty finger-breadths in length by virtue of its unsurpassed purity.

The four types of *gaṇḍī* are to be understood through the classification of the characteristics of the Body (*kāya*). In all respects, through supreme purity, the one hundred and twenty parts are for the purpose of shattering the twenty peaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that have arisen.
The exertion is taught to consist of twenty-four measures;
it is for the purpose of completely shattering the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection. Its width is correctly seen to be twenty-four parts.
The sixteen aspects of the truths are said to be its sixteen parts;
in the middle, there are five parts, consisting of portions that are circular and diminished by only one unit.

It is explained as having sixteen parts by way of the sixteen aspects of the truths. One part of the five central sections is the circular portion, namely the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*jñānadarśana*).
This arrangement of their five portions is due to the purification of the view of a real self (*satkāya*).

The aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the primordial wisdom of the vision of liberation. These are the purification of the view of a transitory collection; therefore, they are presented here as the fivefold portion.

The exertions (*vyāyāma*) are twelve hundred finger-breadths in length, consisting of the aspects of the knowledge of the path through the application of purification; furthermore, they are purified by the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

The one hundred and ten finger-breadths in circumference is the purity of consciousness through its application; its diameter is twenty-two, which is the purity of the twenty-two productions of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*).
Possessing twelve corners, it has the aspect of the nature of dependent origination;
it has the aspect of the cultivation of the path, which is the abandonment of the ninety-eight afflictions.

Its equality with the twelve [links] is the aspect of the *dharmatā* of dependent origination. Its measure is as long as that which consists in the aspect of cultivating the path that thoroughly eliminates the ninety-eight afflictions.
Its length is precisely that measure, its circumference being twentyfold the emptiness;
adorned with eight peaks through the purity of the eight liberations, it is the *gaṇḍī*.
The twenty aspects of emptiness constitute the circular perimeter; the eight liberations, being completely pure, adorn it as the eight corners of the *gaṇḍī*.
It is praised when it measures eighty finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width;
its height corresponds to the [height of the] Dharmaskandha, and its shape is that of the maṇḍala of the unique qualities (āveṇikadharma).
It is taught that it has eighty fingers in height, equal to four finger-widths; its height is the aggregate of dharmas (dharmaskandha), characterized by the distinct qualities of the Dharma.
The circularity [of the body] should be known as measured by eighteen hand-petals (karapallava).
The circumference and height of these [mandalas] increase sequentially according to their respective proportions.
There are eighteen complete enclosures; their extent is known by the palm-leaves. This explanation of their dimensions is the sequence of their breadth and height.
The subtle elements (tanmātrās), which have the sixteen principles as their form, are the supreme and intermediate functions;
the gong (gaṇḍī) consists of those functions and is characterized by the twelve truths.
By way of the sixteen aspects of reality itself, its measure is circular; otherwise, it is in the center. Due to the distinction of the twelve truths, the *gaṇḍī* is circular in nature.

The two pairs of bells of complete purity consist of the two verses beginning with "Exert yourselves! which have the form of proclaiming to the sentient beings of the three realms through rays of light emerging from the root-jewels.

Light rays abide at the base of the jewel; the two verses beginning with "The forms of the voices of sentient beings of the three realms shall be composed" constitute the pair of completely pure bells.
Above that, by means of four, three, two and a half, and two finger-breadths [respectively],
there is a jewel resembling the face of a frog, which is the source of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The tip [of the tongue] should be four, three, two and a half, or two finger-breadths; that which resembles the face of a tortoise is the supreme form of the Buddha’s wisdom.

The best measurement is reduced by three, one, five, and seven [finger-breadths] respectively. Whatever method is considered appropriate for constructing according to these proportions should be employed.
Three, one, five, and seven finger-widths—these measurements are excellent for all inferior [statues]. Regarding the measurements explained here, whatever is suitable to the mind should be employed.
Or rather, it is the gong, radiant with rows of decorative patterns dyed in various colors,
or else bright with red lacquer and producing melodious sounds when struck by a wooden mallet.

Well-anointed with various pigments, and adorned with radiant garlands of colored threads of perfect proportions; born of excellent soil and glowing with vermilion dye, the *gaṇḍī* produces a beautiful sound when struck.
Endowed with a multitude of various virtues, the mantra-practitioner, having performed the rites of bathing and so forth,
should be seated upon a lotus on a pedestal made of gold, gems, and other materials in the northeastern corner.

A mantra practitioner, endowed with a multitude of diverse qualities and skilled in the rituals of ablution and so forth, should place a lotus upon a throne made of gold, precious gems, and the like, situated in the northwestern corner.
First, one should establish the great gong (mahāgaṇḍī), which is endowed with a mallet,
produced from the seed-syllable DHĪḤ, and whose nature is the wisdom of insight (prajñājñāna).
The *gaṇḍī* is first consecrated as being perfectly equal to its handle; it is a great *gaṇḍī* born from the seed-syllable *dhīḥ*, the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) and primordial awareness (*jñāna*).

One should recite it three times with the root mantra beginning with *oṃ dhīḥ śruti-smṛti-ādi*, and with the verse on the purity of the arising of causes (*hetūtpādaviśuddhi*), namely the *Yedharmā-gāthā*.

One should recite one hundred and eight times the root mantra beginning with *oṃ dhīḥ śrutismṛti*, and three times the verse of the *Ye dharmā* which arises from the Tantra, for the sake of complete purification.
It is slightly less than one-third [of its size], subtle, shaped like a mongoose, round on both sides,
fashioned from dense and very hard wood, or else colored with lac and resin.
Small, three-part, fine, and resembling a *nakula*, with a circular shape; fashioned from lovely and solid wood, and further stained with red pigment.
Arising from the seed-syllable of the primordial supreme, perfectly pure in the form of the *ākoṭaka* vajra,
it is twelve finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in circumference.

Arising from the seed-syllable of the Supreme, it is of the nature of the Vajra-knave, utterly pure; it is twelve finger-widths in length and perfectly circular, measuring six finger-widths in circumference.
There is also the purity of the twelvefold limbs of the teaching and the six perfections,
as well as the turning of the wheel of Dharma in both forward and reverse order.

The twelve parts are the branches of the sublime speech; even the six are the very purity of the perfections. When the wheel of the Dharma’s branches is turned, through the modes of forward and reverse progression, {242b3}
Through the purity of emanation and reabsorption, the threefold "slaying" is like the yoga of the six limbs;
it is dissolved into the three bodies by means of the symbolic gesture of saluting the Three Jewels.
In the manner of expanding and withdrawing, strike three times as in the application of the six limbs; then, dissolve into the three bodies and pay homage to the Three Jewels.
In that monastery, according to the prescribed rule, the *smṛti-gaṇḍī* is struck three times, four, or five times every day throughout the day, while maintaining silence.
In the temple, with mindfulness of the ritual, if one strikes the *gaṇḍī* three, four, or five times every day at regular intervals, while meditating on the object of calm abiding (*śamatha*),...
There dwell monks who are abodes of fortitude and endowed with virtuous qualities.
And those who hear this sound shall become the foundation for wealth, progeny, and prosperity.

In that place, the śramaṇas, perfected by a multitude of virtuous qualities, will dwell with steadfast certainty; and wherever their voice is heard, there wealth and a multitude of people will continuously flourish.
The empowerment mantra: Oṃ dhīḥ! To the victory of hearing, memory, intelligence, and understanding; O wisdom, power, intellect, and retention—svāhā!
The mantra for consecration is: oṃ dhīḥ śruti smṛti mati gati vijaye prajñā prajñāvali dhāraṇi svāhā.
The ritual procedure for the characteristics of the gaṇḍī.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the characteristics of Gaṇḍī.
